PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 92 — Lesson 116: Headache, Migraine & Secondary Headache Red Flags

FNP-level goal: Identify a primary headache pattern only after actively considering dangerous secondary causes, use a focused history and examination to decide when emergency imaging or specialist evaluation is needed, and build an individualized migraine plan that improves function while avoiding medication-overuse and treatment-safety harm.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate common clinical patterns of migraine, tension-type headache, cluster headache, and medication-overuse headache.
  • Use onset, age, systemic context, neurologic findings, pregnancy, trauma, eye symptoms, immune status, cancer history, and change in pattern to identify secondary-headache red flags.
  • Perform a focused headache examination including vital signs, neurologic assessment, funduscopic considerations, eye findings, neck evaluation, and medication review.
  • Choose imaging and laboratory evaluation because they answer a defined clinical question, not simply because the patient has pain.
  • Develop a safe acute and preventive migraine strategy, clear return precautions, and referral pathway that respects pregnancy potential, comorbidities, and medication-overuse risk.

Part 1 — First Decide Whether the Headache Could Be Dangerous

Headache is common; missed secondary headache can be catastrophic. The first FNP task is not to choose a migraine drug. It is to ask: Is this sudden, new, changed, systemic, neurologic, traumatic, pregnancy-related, eye-related, or associated with a high-risk host? A thunderclap onset reaching maximum intensity rapidly, new focal neurologic deficit, altered mental status, fever with meningeal symptoms, papilledema concern, pregnancy or postpartum context, cancer or immunocompromise, anticoagulation with trauma, new onset later in life, or a substantial pattern change should trigger a secondary-headache pathway.

Red flags guide urgency but are not a checklist that replaces judgment. A patient can have a history of migraine and still have hemorrhage, stroke, meningitis, glaucoma, venous thrombosis, hypertensive emergency, temporal arteritis, or another new condition. Conversely, not every headache needs imaging. The art is matching the evaluation to the phenotype and risk.

Part 2 — Build a Headache Phenotype

Ask about onset, time to peak, frequency, duration, location, quality, severity, triggers, aura, nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, activity limitation, autonomic symptoms, sleep, menstrual or hormonal association, trauma, positional features, exertional or sexual triggers, Valsalva association, fever, neck stiffness, visual symptoms, focal weakness, speech symptoms, seizures, medications, caffeine, alcohol or other substance use, sleep apnea risk, and family history. Ask what the patient means by worst headache; then ask whether it was maximal immediately or evolved like previous attacks.

Migraine often causes recurrent moderate to severe attacks with features such as unilateral or bilateral throbbing pain, nausea, light or sound sensitivity, and worsening with routine activity. Aura can involve reversible neurologic symptoms, but first, prolonged, atypical, motor, or persistent neurologic symptoms require careful assessment. Tension-type headache is often bilateral pressure or tightness without the full migrainous symptom complex. Cluster headache tends to cause severe unilateral orbital or temporal pain with ipsilateral autonomic features and a circadian or cluster pattern. Do not force a patient into a label when the pattern is mixed or changing.

Part 3 — Focused Examination

Check blood pressure, temperature, general appearance, mental status, cranial nerves, motor and sensory function, coordination, gait when safe, neck range of motion, scalp or temporal artery tenderness when clinically relevant, and eye findings. Evaluate pupils, visual acuity, eye redness, photophobia, and extraocular movements. Consider funduscopic examination when feasible and within skill, especially if raised intracranial pressure is a concern. A normal exam is reassuring only when it fits a nonred-flag history; it does not erase a thunderclap onset or high-risk context.

Medication review is an examination of its own. Ask how many days per month acute medications are used, including over-the-counter analgesics, combination products, caffeine-containing agents, opioids, triptans, and other migraine-specific treatments. Frequent acute-medication use can perpetuate medication-overuse headache and may signal inadequate preventive strategy, not patient noncompliance.

Part 4 — Imaging and Testing With Purpose

Urgent emergency evaluation is appropriate for thunderclap headache, suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, stroke, venous thrombosis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, hypertensive emergency with end-organ findings, severe pregnancy or postpartum headache, or other unstable presentation. Emergency teams select imaging and lumbar-puncture pathways based on timing, examination, and differential. In primary care, do not delay transfer while trying to complete an exhaustive outpatient workup.

For a stable recurrent headache with a consistent primary pattern, normal examination, and no red flags, routine neuroimaging is often not necessary. If the pattern changes, neurologic signs emerge, or a secondary cause becomes plausible, reassess the imaging question. Testing should answer a question: infection, inflammation, metabolic issue, pregnancy, medication toxicity, sleep disorder, visual emergency, or another specific concern.

Part 5 — Acute Migraine Care Is Individualized

Acute treatment selection depends on diagnosis confidence, severity, timing, prior response, contraindications, pregnancy status, cardiovascular and renal risk, drug interactions, frequency of attacks, and patient preference. Early treatment at the onset of an established migraine attack can be more effective than waiting until pain is severe. Nonpharmacologic measures such as hydration, a dark quiet environment, sleep regularity, and trigger awareness can complement—not replace—evidence-based acute treatment.

Some migraine-specific agents are not appropriate for every patient, particularly when vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, pregnancy considerations, or interaction risks exist. New or atypical headache should not be self-treated repeatedly as migraine. The FNP uses current prescribing information and guidelines, documents safety screening, and arranges reassessment when acute treatment is failing or being used too often.

Part 6 — Prevention and Medication-Overuse Safety

Preventive therapy is considered when attacks are frequent, disabling, prolonged, poorly responsive to acute therapy, associated with medication overuse, or meaningfully impair work, caregiving, or quality of life. The best preventive plan considers comorbid hypertension, mood symptoms, sleep, weight, reproductive plans, cardiovascular risk, drug interactions, cost, and patient goals. Keep a headache diary that records frequency, severity, disability, acute medication days, menses or other triggers, and response; it turns vague recall into clinical data.

Medication-overuse headache is not a moral failure. It is a pattern in which frequent use of acute headache medicines contributes to more frequent or persistent headache. Explain the cycle, create a safe withdrawal or transition plan that fits the medication class and patient risk, offer prevention, and schedule follow-up. Do not simply instruct a patient with severe daily use to stop all medication without considering withdrawal, pain, comorbidities, and support.

Part 7 — Special Contexts: Pregnancy, Postpartum, and Older Adults

Pregnancy and postpartum headache require a lower threshold for secondary-cause assessment because hypertensive disorders, thrombosis, hemorrhage, and other conditions may present with headache. Coordinate urgently when headache is severe, new, different, associated with blood-pressure elevation, visual symptoms, neurologic symptoms, or other obstetric warning signs. Medication selection must use pregnancy and lactation-specific information, not a standard migraine algorithm copied unchanged.

A new headache later in life or a major pattern change deserves careful evaluation. Temporal symptoms, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, systemic inflammation, malignancy, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, and head trauma each change the differential and may change urgency. The correct response is tailored escalation, not reflexive reassurance or reflexive imaging of every uncomplicated recurrence.

Part 8 — FNP Case: The Sudden Maximal Headache

A 46-year-old with no previous headache history develops abrupt severe occipital pain that peaks within minutes while lifting a heavy object and is accompanied by neck stiffness. A normal office neurologic screen does not make this safe. The FNP treats the time course as a possible vascular emergency, arranges emergency evaluation, and communicates the onset, exertional trigger, peak timing, and examination findings.

Part 9 — FNP Case: Frequent Migraine and Daily Medication

A 29-year-old has 12 disabling headache days per month and uses a combination analgesic most workdays. The pattern is consistent with migraine but complicated by frequent acute medication exposure. The FNP confirms no red flags, assesses reproductive plans and comorbidities, builds an acute-use limit and prevention discussion, starts or coordinates an individualized evidence-based plan, and schedules close follow-up with a headache diary. More refills alone would not solve the problem.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Postpartum Headache With Visual Symptoms

A patient one week postpartum reports new severe headache, visual spots, and elevated blood pressure. The FNP does not attribute it to sleep deprivation or a prior migraine history. Obstetric and neurologic emergencies are considered, and emergency evaluation is arranged immediately.

FNP High-Yield Framework: HEAD

  1. H — Hear the time course: thunderclap, new, changing, exertional, positional, or progressive patterns matter.
  2. E — Examine for emergency clues: vitals, neurologic status, eyes, neck, systemic illness, pregnancy, trauma, and high-risk host factors.
  3. A — Assign a phenotype only after safety review: migraine, tension-type, cluster, medication overuse, or uncertain.
  4. D — Design a durable plan: individualized acute treatment, prevention when indicated, medication-use limits, diary, referral, and explicit return precautions.

Take-Home Summary

FNP headache care begins with secondary-cause safety, not with a prescription. A consistent primary headache phenotype with a normal appropriate examination can be managed thoughtfully, but thunderclap onset, neurologic findings, systemic illness, pregnancy or postpartum context, eye symptoms, trauma, and major pattern change require escalation. For migraine, success means fewer disability days and less acute-medication reliance, not simply a different rescue drug.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace emergency assessment, neurology or ophthalmology consultation, current prescribing information, or individualized pregnancy and postpartum care. Sudden severe headache, new neurologic deficit, fever with neck stiffness, vision loss or painful red eye, altered mental status, severe pregnancy or postpartum headache, or head trauma with concerning symptoms requires urgent evaluation.
